latin.245: GAR. 2. Nihil in eo mirum quod Adamus & statim a peccato privationem justitiae incurrit, & nec aeterna morte damnatus est, nec temporalem statim sensit. In spiritualem statim incurrit, ita volente Deo, ne si statim in eum non incurrisset ulla species mortis, videri posset Adamo verior Satanae promissio, non moriemini omnino, quam Dei comminatio, morte moriemini; & in peccato consenescens Adamus de seria poenitentia & conversione ad Deum forte non cogitasset: sed pupugit eum praesentis poenae sensus, ut ad Deum resipiscendo rediret, quem rebellando deseruerat. Mortem vero temporalem non statim incurrit, ut poenitendi tempus ipsi concederetur, quod nullum est post mortem. Hanc poenam eodem quo peccavit die Adamus luisset, nisi visum fuisset Deo ob futuram Christi Satisfactionem, spatium dare generi humano ad agendam poenitentiam, inquit Vir Doctus Disput. de lapsu Adami Thes. ultima. Denique aeternam omnino non incurrit, quia erat inter electos Dei, in quos infernus nihil habet juris. Apocal.
latin.246: PLAC. Haec posterior responsio ad secundam Minoris argumenti mei confirmationem spectare videtur: Sed primo eam non attingit; Deinde sese ipsa contradictione implicat; Denique se praebet ridiculam. Sic enim se habebat illa confirmatio, ut eius vim explicem, Cui, quo die peccavit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna, is non est eo die, sicuti Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus. Atqui Adamo, quo die peccavit, non est inflicta mors corporis, nec aeterna. Ergo Adamus non est eo die, sicuti Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus.
latin.247: Nihil potest responderi, nisi, ei quidem inflictam non fuisse mortem corporis & aeternam, sed tamen inflictam fuisse mortem animae positam in privatione justitiae. Sed contra sic insto. Si inflicta ei fuit mors animae, ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Sed non ideo ei inflicta fuit, quia id exigebat comminatio. Ergo ei inflicta mors illa non fuit. Major negari non potest. Minorem probo. Si ideo ei inflicta fuit mors animae, quia id exigebat comminatio, etiam ei inflictae fuerunt mors corporis & aeterna, quia hoc non minus exigebat comminatio. Attamen hae mortes non sunt ei inflictae. Ergo mors animae non est ideo ei inflicta, quia id exigebat comminatio. De minore nulla lis esse potest. Major, quanquam aperte vera est, tamen eo confirmatur, quod non minus mortem corporis & aeternam Deus comminatus fuerat quam spiritualem. Haec igitur si Dei veritas, & justitia exigebant ut eo die Adamo infligeretur, eadem, veritas & justitia, non minus exigebant, ut illae etiam mortes infligerentur eadem die; par, uti vides, ratio est. Quod huic argumentationi dissolvendae accommodatum sit, nihil animadverto in responsione Viri Docti.
latin.248: Ea autem, quod secundum erat eius peccatum, sese contradictione involvit. Nam qui potuisset Adamus retinens justitiam originalem, quae sine dubio injustitiae seu peccato opponitur, consenescere in peccato, manere a Deo aversus, Dei desertor, Deo rebellis? Quid enim erat justitia illa, nisi conversio cordis ad Deum, obedientia habitualis Dei mandatis, constans voluntas obediendi Deo, jusque illi suum tribuendi, qua, hoc ipso quod ipsi inerat, justus erat Adamus? Quis ergo futurum fuisse credat, ut Adamus, nisi amitteret justitiam, consenesceret in peccato? Contra enim consensisset in justitia, si quidem justitiam non amisisset. Se quoque ridiculam praebet haec responsio, cum fingit ablatam fuisse Adamo justitiam, ut ad Deum resipiscendo rediret. Tantum enim abest, ut mors spiritualis medium sit ad resipiscentiam, & conversionem ad Deum, ut eam homini reddat impossibilem, eumque a Deo longissime abducat. Ridiculum etiam mihi videtur, quod dicitur, pupugisse Adamum praesentis illius poenae sensum.
latin.249: Habitus enim non sunt qualitates sensibiles, neque sentiuntur, aut intelliguntur a nobis, nisi quatenus ex antecedentibus aut consequentibus actibus inesse deprehenduntur. Adde quod mors spiritualis, quantum ad veram pietatem attinet, hominem sensu privat, & facultate bene agendi, eumque ad omne bonum opus ineptum, ad omne malum pronum, aversum a Deo, conversum autem ad carnem & ea quae Deus odit, efficit.
latin.250: Temperare mihi non possum quin sextam rationem superioribus adjungam, ductam primum a phrasi illa morte morieris: Nam nullus quod sciam locus extat in scriptura, ubi phrasis illa morte mori de figurata illa morte sit accipienda, quae nihil aliud est quam absentia sanctitatis in anima. Deinde ab ipso nomine mortis, quod in vetere Testamento mihi non occurrit eo sensu, Immo ne in Novo quidem absolute, & sine additamento, nisi forte Luc. ix. 60. sine ut mortui sepeliant suos mortuos: quo tamen loco non videtur Dominus ad privationem originalis justitiae communem omnibus respexisse, sed ad incredulitatem & contumaciam. Cum enim qui non credit jam sit condemnatus Ioh. 3. 18. & super eum ira Dei maneat. Ioh. 3. 36. nihil prohibet incredulum mortuum appellari. Fac tamen eum ad privationem illam respexisse, solemne ei est vocabula transferre a propria & communiter usitata significatione ad spiritualem & metaphoricam lucis Evangelicae ad tempus tegendae causa, in quo eum imitari non debuerunt Apostoli. Iam quis credat primam illam dei legem & comminationem conceptam verbis usitatissimis morte morieris, intelligendam esse sensu prorsus inusitato, & quidem ita ut idem vocabulum semel positum, semel intelligendum, accipiatur simul & proprie, & metaphorice. Possum te obruere aliis argumentis, sed non sunt omnia simul ac semel effundenda.

pass_a.245: GAR. 2. There is nothing wonderful in this, that Adam both at once from the sin incurred the privation of righteousness, and was not damned with eternal death, nor at once felt temporal death. Into spiritual death he at once ran, God so willing, lest if at once no species of death had run upon him, Satan's promise, you will not die at all, might seem to Adam truer than God's threat, by death you will die; and Adam growing old in sin might perhaps not have thought of serious repentance and conversion to God: but the sense of present punishment pricked him, that by repenting he might return to God, whom by rebelling he had deserted. But temporal death he did not at once incur, that time of repenting might be granted him, which is none after death. This punishment Adam would have paid on the same day on which he sinned, unless it had seemed good to God, on account of the future Satisfaction of Christ, to give space to the human race for doing repentance, says the Learned Man, Disputation on the fall of Adam, last Thesis. Finally eternal death he did not incur at all, because he was among the elect of God, over whom hell has no right. Apocalypse.
pass_a.246: PLAC. This later reply seems to look to the second confirmation of the Minor of my argument: But first it does not touch it; Then it entangles itself in contradiction; Finally it shows itself ridiculous. For that confirmation stood thus, that I may unfold its force: He to whom, on the day he sinned, bodily death was not inflicted, nor eternal, is not on that day, as God had threatened, dead. But to Adam, on the day he sinned, bodily death was not inflicted, nor eternal. Therefore Adam is not on that day, as God had threatened, dead.
pass_a.247: Nothing can be answered, except that indeed bodily and eternal death was not inflicted on him, but yet the death of the soul placed in privation of righteousness was inflicted. But against this I press thus. If the death of the soul was inflicted on him, for that reason it was inflicted on him, because the threat required it. But it was not for that reason inflicted on him, because the threat required it. Therefore that death was not inflicted on him. The major cannot be denied. I prove the minor. If for that reason the death of the soul was inflicted on him, because the threat required it, then also bodily and eternal death were inflicted on him, because the threat required this no less. Yet these deaths were not inflicted on him. Therefore the death of the soul is not for that reason inflicted on him, because the threat required it. About the minor there can be no dispute. The major, though openly true, is yet confirmed by this, that God had threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual. If therefore God's truth and justice required that this be inflicted on Adam that day, the same truth and justice required no less that those deaths also be inflicted the same day; the reason, as you see, is equal. What would be suited to dissolving this argumentation I notice nothing of in the Learned Man's reply.
pass_a.248: But that reply, which was the second of his, wraps itself in contradiction. For how could Adam, retaining original righteousness, which without doubt is opposed to unrighteousness or sin, grow old in sin, remain turned away from God, a deserter of God, rebellious toward God? For what was that righteousness, except conversion of the heart to God, habitual obedience to God's commands, a constant will of obeying God, and of rendering him his due, by which, by this very thing that it was in him, Adam was righteous? Who then would believe it would have been, that Adam, unless he lost righteousness, would grow old in sin? For on the contrary he would have grown old in righteousness, if indeed he had not lost righteousness. This reply also shows itself ridiculous, when it feigns that righteousness was taken from Adam so that by repenting he might return to God. For so far is it that spiritual death is a means to repentance and conversion to God, that it renders that impossible for the man, and leads him very far away from God. It also seems ridiculous to me, that it is said the sense of that present punishment pricked Adam.
pass_a.249: For habits are not sensible qualities, nor are they sensed or understood by us, except insofar as from antecedent or consequent acts they are detected to be present. Add that spiritual death, as far as true piety is concerned, deprives the man of sense and of the faculty of acting well, and makes him unfit for every good work, prone to every evil, turned away from God, but turned toward the flesh and those things which God hates.
pass_a.250: I cannot restrain myself from adding a sixth reason to the former ones, drawn first from that phrase by death you shall die: For there exists no place in Scripture that I know, where that phrase to die by death is to be taken of that figured death, which is nothing other than absence of holiness in the soul. Then from the very name of death, which in the Old Testament does not occur to me in that sense, Indeed not even in the New absolutely and without addition, unless perhaps Luke 9:60, leave the dead to bury their dead: in which place yet the Lord does not seem to have looked to the privation of original righteousness common to all, but to unbelief and stubbornness. For since he who does not believe is already condemned John 3:18, and the wrath of God remains upon him John 3:36, nothing prevents calling the unbeliever dead. Grant yet that he looked to that privation, it is solemn for him to transfer words from their proper and commonly used signification to a spiritual and metaphorical one for the sake of covering for a time the light of the Gospel, in which the Apostles ought not to have imitated him. Now who would believe that first law and threat of God, conceived in most usual words by death you shall die, is to be understood in a sense altogether unused, and indeed so that the same word once placed, to be understood once, is taken at once both properly and metaphorically. I could overwhelm you with other arguments, but not all are to be poured out at once and together.

245: Garissoles. 2. No wonder Adam at once lost righteousness by the sin, and yet was not damned to eternal death, nor felt bodily death at once. He fell into spiritual death at once—God willing it—lest, if no kind of death had struck him at once, Satan's promise (you will not die at all) should look truer to Adam than God's threat (you will die the death); and lest Adam, growing old in sin, should never think of serious repentance and return to God. The sting of present punishment pricked him so that he might repent and come back to the God he had left by rebellion.

Bodily death he did not meet at once, so that time to repent might be given him—there is none after death. He would have paid that penalty the very day he sinned, had God not, for Christ's coming Satisfaction, chosen to give the human race space for repentance (so the Learned Man says in his Disputation on Adam's fall, last thesis). Eternal death he never met at all, because he was among God's elect, over whom hell has no claim. (Apocalypse.)
246: Placeus. This later reply seems aimed at the second support of my minor. First it never touches that support. Then it contradicts itself. Finally it turns silly.

The support ran thus: Whoever, on the day he sinned, was not hit with bodily death or eternal death, did not die that day as God had threatened. But Adam, the day he sinned, was not hit with bodily death or eternal death. Therefore Adam did not die that day as God had threatened.
247: The only way out is to say: bodily and eternal death were not laid on him, yet the soul's death—privation of righteousness—was. I press against that. If the soul's death was laid on him, it was laid on him because the threat required it. But it was not laid on him because the threat required it. So that death was not laid on him.

The major stands. For the minor: if the soul's death was laid on him because the threat required it, then bodily and eternal death were laid on him too, for the threat required those no less. Yet those deaths were not laid on him. So the soul's death was not laid on him because the threat required it. The minor is beyond dispute. The major, already plain, is confirmed because God had threatened bodily and eternal death no less than spiritual. If God's truth and justice required the spiritual death that day, the same truth and justice required those other deaths the same day—the reason is the same. I see nothing in the Learned Man's reply that dissolves this.
248: His second point wraps itself in contradiction. How could Adam, still keeping original righteousness—which is the opposite of unrighteousness and sin—grow old in sin, stay turned from God, desert God, rebel against God? What was that righteousness but a heart turned to God, habitual obedience to his commands, a steady will to obey him and give him his due—the very thing that made Adam righteous while it was in him? Who believes Adam would have grown old in sin unless he had lost righteousness? He would have grown old in righteousness if he had kept it.

The reply also turns silly when it pretends righteousness was stripped from Adam so he might repent and return to God. Spiritual death is so far from being a path to repentance and conversion that it makes them impossible and drives the man farthest from God. And it is silly to say the 'sense' of that present penalty pricked Adam.
249: Habits are not sensible qualities. We neither feel nor understand them except as we infer them from acts that go before or follow. Add this: spiritual death, for true piety, strips a man of sense and of the power to do well. It makes him unfit for every good work, ready for every evil, turned from God, and turned to the flesh and to what God hates.
250: I cannot help adding a sixth reason to the ones above, drawn first from the phrase 'you shall die the death.' I know no place in Scripture where 'to die the death' is taken of that figured death which is only absence of holiness in the soul. Next, from the name 'death' itself: I do not find that sense in the Old Testament, and not even in the New used absolutely and without addition—unless perhaps Luke 9:60, 'let the dead bury their dead,' where the Lord seems to mean unbelief and stubbornness, not the privation of original righteousness common to all. For whoever does not believe is already condemned (John 3:18), and God's wrath remains on him (John 3:36)—so an unbeliever may well be called dead.

Grant that he meant that privation: it is his way to shift words from their proper, common sense to a spiritual, metaphorical one, to veil the Gospel light for a time—and the Apostles should not have copied him there. Who then believes God's first law and threat, set in the most ordinary words 'you shall die the death,' must be read in a sense wholly unused—and so that the same word, used once and to be taken once, is taken both properly and metaphorically at once? I could bury you with further arguments, but not everything must be poured out at once.
